summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Electronic Payment Systems Modernization & Digital Fee Infrastructure
summary_responses.response: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposes to require electronic payment of fees and civil penalties, ending the use of cash, money orders and paper checks unless the law authorizes another method. The proposal covers aviation and commercial space transportation penalties, as well as fees for aircraft registration and recording, replacement certificates and test reports, overflights and FAA services abroad. The changes would align FAA regulations with Executive Order 14247 and the agency’s existing practice of directing customers to Pay.gov. The FAA estimates that ending paper payment processing would save it $99,815 annually and expects customers to face minimal transition costs. The public can comment on the proposal through January 4, 2027, using docket number FAA-2026-3538.

summary_responses.subtopic: Aerospace Rotorcraft Structural Engineering & FAA Airworthiness Directives
summary_responses.response: The FAA has proposed an airworthiness directive for certain Airbus EC135 and EC635T2+ helicopters because the manufacturer’s inspection instructions for hard landings are incomplete. Those gaps could allow tail rotor control damage to go undetected, potentially leading to system failure and reduced control of the helicopter. Operators would have to inspect the tail rotor control system once within 12 months of the directive’s effective date, take any necessary corrective action, and update their maintenance instructions and programs. The FAA estimates that the proposal would affect 289 U.S.-registered helicopters and that the inspection and maintenance updates would cost $425 per helicopter, excluding any follow-up work. Public comments are due by January 4, 2027.

summary_responses.subtopic: National Park Administration, Conservation & Multi-Use Trail Regulation
summary_responses.response: A National Park Service rule effective December 21, 2026, will allow Mammoth Cave National Park’s superintendent to designate about 37 miles of multi-use trails for bicycling, up from about 19 miles. The park plans to build eight new multi-use trails, end bicycle access on the White Oak Trail, and close and restore the Maple Springs Connector Trail to its natural condition. The superintendent may also allow e-bikes on designated bicycle trails and will notify the public which routes are open. The rule will permit horseback riding on the 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road, giving riders shorter loop options and access to the river. These changes are part of a broader plan to improve recreation and trail conditions, which the Park Service determined would have no significant environmental impact.
